purpose: Final HELD-OUT retrieval run: every r3 held-out question (easy 103 + hard 97). Aggregates only — never inspect per question.
method: all ids.heldout of MANIFEST.json and MANIFEST-HARD.json (seed-42 stratified splits, r3-PREREG.md); no draw

probes.query: When a write mentions a field name that no group of servers has ever stored, how does the cluster choose which group will hold that field's data, and who records the choice?
expectedFacts: The alpha handling the write asks Zero's ShouldServe to serve the field, proposing its OWN group id as the requested owner.
Zero records the assignment by proposing it through its Raft group; if another group already owns it, the first assignment wins and the existing owner is returned.
Reserved internal predicates are forced onto group 1 by Zero's ShouldServe regardless of which group asked (so that ACL updates stream from one group and restore after a drop-all is simpler).

probes.query: When an administrator updates the application API definition on one server of a multi-node cluster, how do the other servers find out and start serving the new API?
expectedFacts: The update is forwarded to the group-1 leader, which stores the schema text as a value of a reserved predicate on a single schema node and commits it.

Each alpha's admin server starts a background SubscribeForUpdates on that schema predicate's key prefix for group 1; it connects to a group-1 member and receives the updated posting list over a Subscribe stream.

The subscriber callback skips stale versions or unchanged text, regenerates the GraphQL schema, and swaps it in (resetSchema) only if the namespace's schema was already loaded; otherwise it is lazy-loaded later.

probes.query: How does the system decide whether a new backup is a full copy or only the changes since the previous one, and how does a restore then choose which earlier backups to replay?
expectedFacts: ProcessBackupRequest reads the latest manifest at the destination and uses its read timestamp as SinceTs; forceFull sets SinceTs to 0. Type is 'full' when SinceTs is 0, otherwise 'incremental' with BackupNum incremented under the same BackupId.
An incremental backup is refused if the new read ts does not advance past the last manifest, or if encryption is on for one side and off for the other (forceFull is the suggested escape).

getManifestsToRestore keeps only manifests whose backup files all exist, walks from the newest back to the latest full backup (optionally filtered by BackupId), and verifyManifests checks the BackupNum chain is consecutive starting at 1.

probes.query: An end user of the GraphQL API sends a signed token in a request header. Follow how the claims inside that token end up restricting the database query generated for that request.
expectedFacts: The resolver calls AttachAuthorizationJwt, which reads the header named in the schema's authorization metadata, strips a 'Bearer ' prefix and stores the token in incoming gRPC metadata.
ExtractCustomClaims validates the token (HS/RS key or JWK URLs, audience check) and flattens the namespace claim into AuthVariables; with closed-by-default and no token it errors.

queryRewriter.Rewrite passes AuthVariables to the authRewriter, which evaluates claim-only (RBAC) rules statically and turns data-dependent rules into extra DQL queries/filters using those variable values.

The default is applied only on the regular ordered path; ordering by a facet or by a value variable returns earlier through their own functions.

probes.query: Can the database engine be used inside another Go program without running a separate cluster-coordinator process, and what must the host program supply?
expectedFacts: Yes: an embedded mode is switched on with hooks.Enable(cfg), and the host supplies an implementation of ZeroHooks.
ZeroHooks covers five coordinator operations: assigning UIDs, timestamps and namespace IDs, committing or aborting a transaction, and applying mutations.
When embedded mode is off or no hooks are given, GetHooks returns the default network-backed implementation registered by the worker package's init.

probes.query: Where do change-data events for external consumers come from, and why was that source chosen over subscribing to the key-value store directly?
expectedFacts: Events are built by reading the Raft write-ahead log on the group leader, not from Badger subscriptions.
The stated reason: if the sink (e.g. Kafka) connection is lost the job can resume from the last sent event and keep events in commit order, which a Badger scan cannot guarantee.
Mutation events are held per start timestamp and sent only when the commit delta arrives, carrying the commit ts; the only sinks are Kafka and a file.

probes.query: Where is a write rejected because a long text value would produce search-index entries too big for the underlying key-size limit?
expectedFacts: validateMutation computes maxSizeForDataKey = 65000 - len(predicate) and skips edges whose value is no longer than that.
Only string-typed predicates are checked; for each tokenizer on the predicate the tokens are built and any token longer than the limit returns 'value in the mutation is too large for the index'.

probes.query: When a non-admin user reads a field they hold no permission for, is the whole request rejected or is the field quietly dropped, and where is that decided?
expectedFacts: authorizeQuery gets the blocked predicates from AuthorizePredicates and removes them (and variables derived from them) from the parsed query via removePredsFromQuery; the rest of the request still runs.
AclCache.AuthorizePredicate denies by default: a predicate with no matching group rule gives 'unauthorized to do read on predicate ...', unless a dgraph.all rule applies.
Guardians skip this check (unless shared-instance blocks ACL predicates), and ACL predicates are blocked for everyone else.

probes.query: When a read needs data held by another group of servers and the first replica answers slowly, what does the calling server do?
expectedFacts: If the local node serves the group no network call is made; otherwise up to two members of the group are chosen.
The request goes to the first; if no reply arrives within one second (backupRequestGracePeriod) the same request is also sent to the second, and the first successful reply wins.
If the first fails before the grace period, the second is tried immediately.

probes.query: How does result sorting choose between walking a sorted index and fetching the values directly?
expectedFacts: processSort does not choose up front: it runs both strategies concurrently and takes the first to finish without error.
The value-fetching strategy is started only after a 3 ms delay, so a quick index sort usually wins; the loser is cancelled through the shared context.
If the first to return has an error the other result is used; sorting on list-typed predicates and negative counts are rejected beforehand.

probes.query: Where does the query engine implement built-in whole-graph analytics such as PageRank or connected-component detection?
expectedFacts: Not implemented: the only graph-wide algorithms are the recurse traversal (query/recurse.go) and shortest path with optional k paths (query/shortest.go, Dijkstra-based).
Everything else is per-query traversal, filtering, aggregation and group-by.

The query package contains aggregator, arena, groupby, math, mutation, outputnode*, outputrdf, query, recurse, shortest and tables only; none is an analytics algorithm.

The only periodic jobs in the worker package are housekeeping tickers (tablet sizes, snapshots, cleanup), none triggers a backup.

probes.query: Where are full-text search results ranked by a relevance score such as BM25 or TF-IDF?
expectedFacts: Not implemented: the full-text functions (alloftext, anyoftext) return boolean matches; allof* is an intersection and anyof* a union of index posting lists, returned in UID order.
Users can only reorder with orderasc/orderdesc on a field; no term-frequency or scoring data is stored in the index.
The only scored ranking is vector similarity search (similar_to over HNSW vector indexes), which ranks by vector distance, not by text relevance.

probes.query: When I push a bookmark, how does jj make sure it does not overwrite something a teammate pushed to that same remote branch after my last fetch? Where is the expected remote value recorded, and how is that expectation enforced during the push?
expectedFacts: push_updates records, per ref, the expected pre-push remote location (the update's 'before' target, which GitRefUpdate documents as sourced from the local remote-tracking bookmark; None if the ref should not exist) and pairs it with the refspec in RefToPush.
spawn_push runs git push with one --force-with-lease=<ref>:<expected-oid> argument per ref (empty oid when the ref is expected not to exist), so git performs the test-and-set.
The refspecs are given in non-forced format because a forced refspec would ignore the lease; jj also passes --no-verify so Git hooks do not run.

probes.query: If two jj processes commit against the same repository at the same moment, so that the operation history forks, what reconciles the fork the next time the repository is opened, and what role does locking play if a third process is doing the same thing concurrently?
expectedFacts: RepoLoader::load_at_head calls resolve_op_heads; with a single head it is used directly, otherwise resolve_op_heads takes the op-heads store lock and re-reads the heads.
Heads that are ancestors of other heads are filtered out via dag_walk_async::heads; if multiple remain, a resolver closure creates a merge operation described as 'reconcile divergent operations'.

merge_operations merges the views of the heads using closest common ancestor operations and rebases descendants; the lock is taken only so concurrent processes do not each produce another set of divergent heads.

probes.query: When uploading commits to a Gerrit server, how does jj derive the review identifier it adds to each commit message, and why does that identifier not show up in my local commit descriptions afterwards?

probes.query: Sometimes the abbreviated commit or change ID that jj displays is longer than needed to be unique among all commits. What extra condition makes jj lengthen it?
expectedFacts: After computing the shortest unique prefix among commits/changes, shortest_commit_prefix_len and shortest_change_prefix_len pass the length through disambiguate_prefix_with_refs.
disambiguate_prefix_with_refs increases the length until the prefix no longer equals the name of a local tag or local bookmark.
This is because tags and bookmarks take priority when resolving a symbol, so a prefix equal to such a name would resolve to the ref instead of the commit.

probes.query: I copied a whole repository directory to a new location, and my per-repo settings seem to be independent now, not shared with the original. Where is the per-repo settings file actually kept, and what logic decides that a copy gets its own settings file?

probes.query: I drop a 5 MB generated file into my working directory. jj does not include it in my commit and prints a hint. Where is that refusal decided, and where does the size limit come from?
expectedFacts: process_dir_entry leaves a new (not yet tracked) file untracked with UntrackedReason::FileTooLarge when its size exceeds max_new_file_size and it is not force-tracked; files already tracked are not affected.

probes.query: Several color rules in the configuration can match the same piece of output, for example one keyed on a single label and another on a label combination. How does jj decide which style wins and how are they combined?
expectedFacts: Rules come from the [colors] table; each key is a space-separated list of labels that must appear in order (as a subsequence) within the current label stack.
Matches are ranked by the reversed list of matched label indices compared lexicographically, so a rule matching later (innermost) labels, such as 'a d' vs 'd' or 'a b c', takes precedence.

All matching styles are sorted by that priority and merged in ascending order, so higher-priority rules override individual attributes while unset attributes from lower rules remain; results are cached per label stack.

probes.query: I fetch several specific branches at once and one of them no longer exists on the remote. How does the fetch logic keep going for the rest, and what happens to my stale remote-tracking copy of the missing branch?
expectedFacts: GitFetch::fetch loops: it runs git fetch, and if git reports a missing remote ref (GitFetchStatus::NoRemoteRef), it removes that refspec from the list and retries with the remaining refspecs.
For each failed refs/heads/<name> it records '<remote>/<name>' in branches_to_prune, because git does not prune on a missing-ref failure even with --prune.
After the loop, spawn_branch_prune deletes those remote-tracking branches with 'git branch --remotes --delete'.

probes.query: Where does jj handle Git LFS pointer files, for example swapping pointers for the real large content when files are checked out or recorded?

probes.query: In what order do user-supplied HTTP wrappers, tracing, resilience handling and the overall time limit surround the actual outgoing network call, and which two components arrange that order?
expectedFacts: DelegatingHandlerFactory.Get builds the list in this order: global handlers not named in the route's handler list, then the route's named handlers sorted by configured order, then the tracing handler (if tracing is enabled), then the QoS handler (if QoS is enabled).

MessageInvokerPool.CreateMessageInvoker reverses that list and sets each handler's InnerHandler, so the last list item (QoS) wraps the SocketsHttpHandler directly and the first list item is the outermost of these handlers.
A TimeoutDelegatingHandler is added on top of the whole chain, so the route timeout covers every handler including QoS.

probes.query: How long does the gateway wait for a backend to reply when nothing is configured, and what happens if one of the explicitly listed routes sets the waiting time to zero or a negative number?

probes.query: Where does the gateway revalidate a stored response with the origin using an entity tag or last-modified timestamp, and answer callers with 'not modified'?
expectedFacts: No conditional-request or entity-tag handling exists; the output cache stores full responses keyed by an MD5 of method, URL, optional header value and optional body, with a fixed TTL, and never revalidates.
NotModified appears only in HttpContextResponder, where a downstream 304 response simply skips writing a body.

filterMapByMeaning picks the reflection whose comment label equals the given label, otherwise picks the element at the given index (default 0) from the keyword-resolved list, which for a function is its list of signatures.
The label comes from a label inline tag in the signature's comment, extracted into comment.label by the Comment constructor.

probes.query: For a function that has several overload signatures plus a body, which doc comment is treated as belonging to the function as a whole? How does that differ from a function with just one signature?
expectedFacts: For overloaded functions, methods or constructors (more than one matching declaration), discoverCommentWorker clears the candidate list and uses only the declaration that has a body (the implementation) as the symbol-level comment source.
For a function with a single signature, the candidate list is cleared and nothing is pushed, so the function reflection itself gets no comment and its signature owns the comment.
Signatures get their comments through a separate discovery path (discoverSignatureComment), and a variable that merely holds call signatures is handled like a normal variable.

probes.query: A big descriptive comment sits at the very top of an entry file, above the first statement. Where does the tool decide whether it describes the whole module or just that first statement, and what marks the difference?
expectedFacts: getCommentImpl, for a module-level comment, discards the comment unless it has the @packageDocumentation modifier or a @module tag, because otherwise it belongs to the first statement in the file.

probes.query: When the server is configured to trace itself, how do its own spans reach the configured storage, and what stops the act of saving them from producing more traces?
expectedFacts: LocalSender.send decodes each JSON-encoded span and calls the storage span consumer's accept(...).execute() directly in-process, with no HTTP hop.
LocalSender.delegate looks the StorageComponent bean up lazily and, when it is a TracingStorageComponent, unwraps it to the underlying storage, so the flush is not itself traced.

TracingStorageComponent wraps storage calls in TracedCall spans for reads and writes; the Tracing bean uses NEVER_SAMPLE and only the HTTP server sampler starts traces (for paths under /api or /zipkin/api).

probes.query: Legacy log messages arrive over a raw TCP socket as length-prefixed frames, possibly many at once. How are those frames cut, decoded into spans, and kept in order in the replies?
expectedFacts: NettyScribeServer installs a LengthFieldBasedFrameDecoder (4-byte length prefix, stripped) in front of ScribeInboundHandler.

ScribeInboundHandler.channelRead wraps each frame as an HTTP thrift request to a THttpService and numbers it; a response is written immediately only if its index is previouslySent+1, otherwise it is parked in pendingResponses and flushed in order by flushResponses.

ScribeSpanConsumer.Log skips entries whose category differs from the configured one, base64 (MIME) decodes the ISO-8859-1 message, decodes a Thrift span with SpanBytesDecoder.THRIFT.decodeOne, then calls collector.accept on the blocking executor.

probes.query: Cassandra storage keeps tables of known service and span names. How does it avoid issuing an insert for the same pair on every batch of spans?
expectedFacts: CassandraSpanConsumer builds insertServiceSpan as an InsertEntry.Factory (a DeduplicatingInsert.Factory) with the autocomplete TTL and cardinality, and accept() calls insertServiceSpan.maybeAdd for each (service, span) pair.

maybeAdd only creates the insert call when DelayLimiter.shouldInvoke returns true; the DelayLimiter suppresses the same context until its TTL expires, bounded by a maximum cardinality where the eldest suppression is evicted.
If the insert fails or is cancelled, DeduplicatingInsert invalidates the context in the DelayLimiter so it will be retried on a later batch.

probes.query: Where is the tail-based sampling logic that, after a whole trace is assembled, keeps traces that contain errors or slow spans?
expectedFacts: The repository has only head-style sampling: CollectorSampler decides per span from the trace ID alone (lower 64 bits compared with a rate boundary; debug spans always kept), applied in Collector.sample before storage.
Nothing buffers a trace until complete before deciding; self-tracing uses Brave samplers for the server's own requests.

probes.query: Besides a client choosing to roll back, list the different situations in which the cluster itself forces a transaction to fail or disappear, and say where each is decided. Count only decisions made by server code, across both the coordinator and the data servers.

probes.query: A team lets each dependency be fetched either as an archive or as a version-control checkout. They choose per package-name pattern, with a catch-all entry, in both their user-level and their project-level settings. Trace how those two layers of settings are combined, how the resulting patterns reach the component that fetches packages, how that component picks the first origin to try for a package that tracks a development branch, and what happens when that first origin fails. Include how an explicit command-line preference interacts with the patterns.
expectedFacts: CRITICAL: Config::merge handles the preferred-install key specially: a plain string value is turned into a map with the catch-all pattern, new values are combined with array_merge (patterns already present keep their position, new patterns from the later layer are appended after the earlier layer's patterns), and the catch-all entry is moved to the end so it is matched last.

Factory::createDownloadManager calls DownloadManager::setPreferences only when the configured value is an array; when it is the plain string 'dist' or 'source' it sets the prefer-dist or prefer-source flag instead.

DownloadManager::resolvePackageInstallPreference walks the pattern map in order, turns '*' into a case-insensitive anchored regex wildcard, and the first match wins: 'dist' gives dist, 'auto' gives dist for stable packages and source for dev packages, anything else gives source; with no match a dev package gets source and a stable package gets dist.

CRITICAL: DownloadManager::getAvailableSources lists source before dist by default and reverses to dist-first only when prefer-source is false and (prefer-dist is true or the pattern result is dist); on updates it keeps the previously installed package's source if the new package offers it, except when a stable dist install is replaced by a dev version.

Command-line choices reach the manager through BaseCommand::getPreferredInstallOptions and Installer::run, which calls setPreferSource and setPreferDist on the DownloadManager before downloading, so an explicit flag takes priority over the pattern map.

DownloadManager::download retries with the next origin only when the next origin is 'dist' (a source failure may fall back to dist); a dist failure is rethrown without falling back to source, and an IrrecoverableDownloadException is never retried.

probes.query: After a login, application code asks the framework to issue a brand-new session identifier for the same visitor. If the session needs a change it calls SessionManager::changeSessionId, then adds a session cookie with the new identifier (path '/', configured SameSite, max-age only when it is >= 0) to that response, using a temporary copy when the response is a shared cached object (HttpAppFrameworkImpl.cc:728-770).

SessionManager::changeSessionId gets the new identifier from the id-generator callback, inserts the same Session object under the new key (CacheMap::insert fires the session-start advice for the new key), and asks the session CacheMap to erase the old key with runAfter(10, ...) (SessionManager.cc:116-127; CacheMap.h:217-247).

CRITICAL: With a positive session timeout, the session CacheMap ticks once per second, so the old key stays about 10 seconds (low precision): a request carrying the old cookie still finds the same Session through getSession, and CacheMap::erase fires the session-destroy advice for the old identifier only when that delay ends (SessionManager.cc:31-67; CacheMap.h:387-396, 417-421).

With the default session timeout of 0 (sessions never expire), the session CacheMap is built with no tick and no wheels, so runAfter cannot schedule the task: the CallbackEntry is released at once and its destructor runs the erase immediately. The old identifier stops working at once (a request with it gets a new, empty session) and the destroy advice fires during handleSessionForResponse (SessionManager.cc:69-85; CacheMap.h:39-49, 417-421, 470-506).

CRITICAL: Database.cancel sets Suspension.isCancelled and, when interruptsWhenCancelled is true, calls sqlite3_interrupt on the connection, which makes the running statement stop (Database.swift:1245-1268).
Statement stepping (executeAllSteps, forEachStep, step) sends any step result other than ROW/DONE to Database.statementDidFail (Statement.swift:566-623).

CRITICAL: For SQLITE_INTERRUPT or SQLITE_ABORT, Database.statementDidFail calls suspensionMutex.load().checkCancellation(), which throws CancellationError when the access is cancelled and interruptsWhenCancelled is true, before any DatabaseError is built (Database+Statements.swift:497-503; Database.swift:370-374).

A statement that starts after the cancellation never runs: statementWillExecute calls checkForSuspensionViolation, which tests the cancelled flag before the suspended flag and throws CancellationError (Database+Statements.swift:449; Database.swift:1388-1393, 1427-1428).

When the access ends, its defer block clears the state with db.uncancel(); DatabasePool.barrierWriteWithoutTransaction (async) repeats the same pattern (SerializedDatabase.swift:258-262; DatabasePool.swift:812-830).

probes.query: A multi-reader database is observed for changes to a query result. The first value must arrive quickly even while a long write is running, yet no change that lands between that first read and the start of listening may be missed. Explain the mechanism step by step, and say what the code falls back to on builds or files where the needed SQLite version-comparison feature is unavailable.
expectedFacts: DatabasePool._add sends a plain observation of a writable pool to _addConcurrent, which creates a ValueConcurrentObserver whose start() reads the initial value from a reader instead of waiting for the writer (DatabasePool.swift:732-777; ValueConcurrentObserver.swift:234-277).

CRITICAL: With snapshot support, the initial read runs inside a long-lived WALSnapshotTransaction obtained from DatabasePool.walSnapshotTransaction: a deferred read transaction on a reader that also records a WALSnapshot of that moment (WALSnapshotTransaction.swift:66-86; DatabasePool.swift:689-701).

CRITICAL: asyncStartObservation then runs on the writer queue, takes a WALSnapshot of the writer connection and compares it with the initial one (sqlite3_snapshot_cmp via WALSnapshot.compare); if the writer's is newer, or the writer's snapshot cannot be taken, it assumes a change, fetches again from the writer and notifies a fresh value; otherwise it only starts observing (ValueConcurrentObserver.swift:423-520, comparison at :451-460; WALSnapshot.swift:89-91).
The snapshot transaction is closed right after the comparison so that its reader returns to the pool (ValueConcurrentObserver.swift:464).

Without snapshot support (compiled without SQLITE_ENABLE_SNAPSHOT or with SQLITE_DISABLE_SNAPSHOT, which Package.swift defines on Linux) the #else branch sends syncStart and asyncStart to the WithoutWALSnapshot variants, which always fetch a second time from the writer after observation starts, so the same value can be notified twice (ValueConcurrentObserver.swift:279, 527-537, 543-700; Package.swift:17-19).

At run time, if the snapshot cannot be created (SQLITE_ERROR: missing or empty WAL file) the observer degrades to the same without-snapshot path; Database.setUpWALMode therefore creates and drops a small table to guarantee a non-empty WAL file (ValueConcurrentObserver.swift:296-300, 411-418; Database.swift:531-562).

probes.query: While SQLite compiles each SQL statement, GRDB learns several kinds of facts about it through SQLite's permission-check callback. List each kind of fact the library keeps for a statement, and for each name the component that later uses it and what it uses it for.
expectedFacts: CRITICAL: Read access (SQLITE_READ) builds selectedRegion, stored as Statement.databaseRegion; it records what a statement reads: Database.statementWillExecute passes it to registerAccess(to:), which feeds the region that ValueObservation records while fetching, and FetchRequest.databaseRegion(_:) returns it when a request is used as an observed region (either consumer is acceptable) (StatementAuthorizer.swift:115-125; Statement.swift:162; Database+Statements.swift:452; Database.swift:934-937; FetchRequest.swift:104).

CRITICAL: Write effects (INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, including trigger and foreign-key-action effects) build databaseEventKinds, stored as Statement.authorizerEventKinds; TransactionObservation.statementObservation(for:) uses them to decide which observers, and which events, are activated for the statement, and canDeleteRows makes Database.add/remove(transactionObserver:) evict cached statements that delete (StatementAuthorizer.swift:127-161; TransactionObserver.swift:44-45, 66-67, 1045-1090).

The schema-changing flag (DROP, CREATE, ALTER, ATTACH, DETACH, and the sqlite_drop_column function before SQLite 3.38) becomes Statement.invalidatesDatabaseSchemaCache; Database.statementDidExecute then clears the schema cache (StatementAuthorizer.swift:98-113, 186-203; Database+Statements.swift:461-464).

The transaction or savepoint effect becomes Statement.transactionEffect: DatabaseObservationBroker.statementDidExecute uses it to maintain the savepoint stack and to detect empty transactions, checkForSuspensionViolation lets rollbacks and read-only commits through, and Statement.releasesDatabaseLock builds on it (StatementAuthorizer.swift:163-185; TransactionObserver.swift:389-430; Database.swift:1367-1374; Statement.swift:808-824).

The query-only pragma flag becomes Statement.isQueryOnlyPragma, which checkForSuspensionViolation uses to let that pragma run even when the database is suspended (StatementAuthorizer.swift:204-207; Database.swift:1378-1380).

Besides recording, the callback returns SQLITE_IGNORE for DELETE on tables whose deletions some observer watches, which disables SQLite's truncate optimization so individual row deletions reach the update hook (StatementAuthorizer.swift:132-155).

probes.query: Two full-text virtual table integrations can keep their index in step with an ordinary table by means of triggers. A maintainer wants to remove the automatic upkeep for the variant whose upkeep uses only after-event triggers (no before-event ones). Which public helper removes it, which trigger names does it drop, where are those triggers created and at what moment of the table-creation flow, and what runs right after they are created?
expectedFacts: CRITICAL: The helper is Database.dropFTS5SynchronizationTriggers(forTable:); it drops the three triggers named __<table>_ai, __<table>_ad and __<table>_au (FTS5.swift:536-541).

CRITICAL: Those triggers are created by FTS5.database(_:didCreate:using:) when the definition is synchronized with a content table (set by FTS5TableDefinition.synchronize(withTable:)); all three are AFTER INSERT, AFTER DELETE and AFTER UPDATE triggers, and delete or update remove old entries by inserting a row with the special 'delete' command into the index table (FTS5.swift:226-280, 472-474).

Database.create(virtualTable:...) runs CREATE VIRTUAL TABLE and then calls module.database(_:didCreate:using:), both inside inSavepoint, so the triggers appear in the same atomic step as the table (VirtualTableModule.swift:182-187).

Right after the triggers, the code runs the 'rebuild' command on the index table so already existing content rows are indexed; temporary external-content tables are refused with a fatal error (FTS5.swift:232-241, 281).

The other variant's helper, dropFTS4SynchronizationTriggers, drops four triggers (__<table>_bu, _bd, _au, _ai: two BEFORE and two AFTER) and deletes old entries with a plain DELETE by docid, so it is not the one asked about (FTS4.swift:136-153, 404-410).

probes.query: A record type has a property that is a list of small structs, and each struct holds a point in time. When the record is written to the database, in what form does that time end up in the stored text, and which piece of code chooses that form? How does it differ from a point-in-time property declared directly on the record?
expectedFacts: CRITICAL: RecordEncoder.encode(_:forKey:) first tries a single-value ColumnEncoder; when the value encodes into a keyed or unkeyed container (as an array of structs does), ColumnEncoder sets requiresJSON, a JSONRequiredError is thrown, and the value is encoded again as JSON (EncodableRecord+Encodable.swift:119-166, 244-275).

CRITICAL: The JSON is produced with Record.databaseJSONEncoder(for: key); its default dateEncodingStrategy is .millisecondsSince1970, so the nested time is stored as a number of milliseconds since 1970 (also base64 data, sorted keys, non-finite floats throw) (EncodableRecord.swift:236-247).
The JSON bytes are turned into a String and persisted as the column value (EncodableRecord+Encodable.swift:159-160).

A Date property declared directly on the record bypasses the JSON encoder: it goes through databaseDateEncodingStrategy(for:), whose default .deferredToDate uses Date's DatabaseValueConvertible text 'yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm:ss.SSS' in UTC (EncodableRecord+Encodable.swift:125-128; EncodableRecord.swift:253-257; Date.swift:155-160).

Look-alikes that are not used here: DatabaseValueConvertible.databaseJSONEncoder() (same defaults, only for values that are both DatabaseValueConvertible and Encodable) and JSONDumpFormat.defaultEncoder (debug dump output) (DatabaseValueConvertible.swift:118-126; DatabaseValueConvertible+Encodable.swift:142; JSONDumpFormat.swift:55-65).
probes.author: r3hb-grdb-drafter
probes.notes: VERIFICATION: EncodableRecord+Encodable.swift:119-166 (encode(_:forKey:): Data/Date/UUID/DatabaseValueConvertible first, then ColumnEncoder try, catch JSONRequiredError -> :151 Record.databaseJSONEncoder(for: key.stringValue).encode(value), :159-160 persist(jsonString)), :244-275 (ColumnEncoder.requiresJSON set in container(keyedBy:) and unkeyedContainer()); EncodableRecord.swift:236-247 (default databaseJSONEncoder: .base64, .millisecondsSince1970, .throw, .sortedKeys, userInfo), :253-257 (databaseDateEncodingStrategy default .deferredToDate); Core/Support/Foundation/Date.swift:45-50, :155-160 (UTC 'yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm:ss.SSS'); no Array/Dictionary DatabaseValueConvertible extension exists (grep 'extension Array' -> only Cursor.swift:56 Dictionary and Row.swift ArrayRowImpl), so arrays take the JSON path. CHEAPEST ROUTE (5 dependent steps): (1) grep 'Codable record' / 'nested' -> docs (Documentation/*.md) and FetchableRecord+Decodable; (2) find the encoding side: EncodableRecord+Encodable.swift; (3) read RecordEncoder.encode -> JSON fallback -> databaseJSONEncoder(for:); (4) open EncodableRecord.swift:236 for the date strategy; (5) compare with direct Date path -> databaseDateEncodingStrategy and Date.swift. FIRST 3 GREPS of the question's words: 'point in time' / 'time' (hundreds), 'list of structs' (no hits), 'stored text' (docs). The question names neither 'JSON' nor 'millisecond' nor 'encoder', so grepping its words reaches only docs/tests; code is found only by guessing that nested values need JSON. DECOYS: DatabaseValueConvertible.databaseJSONEncoder() (DatabaseValueConvertible.swift:118; same defaults; used by DatabaseValueConvertible+Encodable.swift:142 for standalone values), JSONDumpFormat.defaultEncoder (Dump/DumpFormats/JSONDumpFormat.swift:55; no date strategy), FetchableRecord.databaseJSONDecoder(for:) (decoding side), docs Documentation/JSON*.md. Closed-book risk: a model might say ISO 8601 from general Codable habits. est. turns: 6.

probes.query: A developer registers schema-change steps using the default referential-integrity setting. One step is registered, then the migrator is switched to its unsafe, faster mode, then a second step is registered. For each of the two steps, on a connection that has referential constraints turned on and on a connection that has them turned off, what does the library run before, during and after the step?
expectedFacts: CRITICAL: The migrator's option is read when a step is registered, not when it runs: registerMigration maps .deferred to Migration.ForeignKeyChecks.deferred if defersForeignKeyChecks is still true, and to .disabled otherwise; the earlier step keeps .deferred, the later step gets .disabled (DatabaseMigrator.swift:157-159, 319-340).

CRITICAL: On a connection with foreign keys ON, the earlier (deferred) step runs with foreign_keys switched OFF, inside an immediate transaction; after the step and the bookkeeping insert, db.checkForeignKeys() verifies the data before COMMIT, and foreign_keys is switched back ON in a finally block (Migration.swift:34-37, 79-109).

On a connection with foreign keys ON, the later (disabled) step runs the same way (foreign_keys OFF, immediate transaction, ON again in finally) but with no checkForeignKeys call, so violations are not detected (Migration.swift:64-77).

On a connection with foreign keys OFF, Migration.run takes the else branch for both steps: an immediate transaction with the migration and the bookkeeping, no pragma changes and no check (Migration.swift:34, 43-45, 56-62).

A step registered with foreignKeyChecks .immediate always maps to .immediate, whatever the migrator option, and runs in an immediate transaction without toggling the pragma (DatabaseMigrator.swift:327-329; Migration.swift:56-62). All paths run inside db.withSchemaSource(nil) (Migration.swift:33).
probes.author: r3hb-grdb-drafter
probes.notes: VERIFICATION: DatabaseMigrator.swift:113 (defersForeignKeyChecks = true), :157-159 (disablingDeferredForeignKeyChecks returns a copy with the flag false; doc says 'newly registered migrations'), :312-342 (registerMigration: :321-326 deferred -> deferred|disabled by the flag captured now, :327-328 immediate -> immediate); Migration.swift:29-47 (run: PRAGMA foreign_keys query at :34; switch at :35-42; else immediate at :43-45), :56-62 (runWithImmediate), :64-77 (runWithDisabled), :79-109 (runWithDeferred: foreign_keys=OFF :85, inTransaction(.immediate) :89, checkForeignKeys :98, ON in finally :107). CHEAPEST ROUTE (5 dependent steps): (1) grep 'foreign key' + 'migrat' -> DatabaseMigrator.swift and Migration.swift; (2) read DatabaseMigrator.registerMigration for the mapping; (3) notice the flag is read at registration, order matters; (4) read Migration.run for the pragma branch; (5) read the three runWith* bodies to state before/during/after for each. FIRST 3 GREPS of the question's words: 'referential' (no code hits), 'migrator' (DatabaseMigrator.swift = gold), 'schema change'. The question avoids 'foreign key', 'deferred', 'disabling', but 'migrator' reaches the gold file at grep 1 (acknowledged); the order-of-registration trap and the second layer (Migration.run) are what make it a 5-step question. DECOYS: Database.checkForeignKeys() (the verification, not the decision), Database.foreignKeyViolations, Configuration.foreignKeysEnabled (opens the connection with the pragma ON; the question's 'turned on' is a runtime state read by Migration.run), DatabaseMigrator.ForeignKeyChecks (public enum has only deferred/immediate, the private Migration.ForeignKeyChecks also has disabled). est. turns: 6.

probes.query: An application sets, on the configuration shared by all its connections, how a connection should behave when another process holds the file lock: fail at once, wait a fixed time, or run a custom callback. Can the application use that setting to control the reader connections that a multi-reader database pool opens? If so, point to where it is applied to them.
expectedFacts: CRITICAL: No: for pool readers the user's busy setting is never applied. Database.setupBusyMode chooses configuration.readonlyBusyMode ?? configuration.busyMode for read-only connections, which looks as if busyMode reaches readers (Database.swift:580-584).

CRITICAL: DatabasePool.readerConfiguration sets readonly = true on the reader configuration and, because readonlyBusyMode is nil, assigns .timeout(10) to it, so every reader waits up to 10 seconds whatever busyMode says (DatabasePool.swift:114-143; also used for makeSnapshot at DatabasePool.swift:946-950).

readonlyBusyMode is an internal property with no public setter, so the application cannot override the 10-second reader wait; DatabaseSnapshotPool.configure does the same default (Configuration.swift:333-335; DatabaseSnapshotPool.swift:236-254).

The public Configuration.busyMode (default .immediateError) therefore governs only the writer connection of a pool and the connections of a DatabaseQueue (Configuration.swift:326-331; Database.swift:585-607).

probes.notes: VERIFICATION (negative): grep -rn 'busyMode' GRDB -> Configuration.swift:331 (public var), Database.swift:582-583 (setupBusyMode), no other readers; grep -rn 'readonlyBusyMode' GRDB -> Configuration.swift:335 (internal declaration), DatabasePool.swift:137-138, DatabaseSnapshotPool.swift:250-251, Database.swift:582 (only these 4 uses; no assignment from user-visible API); grep -rn 'sqlite3_busy_timeout\|sqlite3_busy_handler' GRDB -> Database.swift:590 and :595 only (inside setupBusyMode); grep -rn 'BusyMode' GRDB -> enum at Database.swift:2022-2040. DatabasePool.swift:114-143 (readerConfiguration), :56-63 (reader config built from it), :946-950 (makeSnapshot uses it); DatabaseSnapshotPool.swift:236-254. FIRST 3 GREPS of the question's words: 'lock' (hundreds), 'busy' (Configuration.swift, Database.swift, DatabaseError.swift codes), 'reader' (hundreds). The question has no 'busyMode' or 'timeout', and a reader who greps 'busy' finds Database.setupBusyMode which seems to answer yes. probes.query: A site publishes, in its name-server data, key material that lets clients hide the destination site name inside the TLS greeting. The server later rotates that key and refuses the client's greeting. Starting from the name-server answer, trace how the key material reaches the TLS handshake, which platform code supplies corrected material after the refusal, and which checks can stop the second attempt. Name the file and component for each step.
expectedFacts: RouteSelector.dnsLookup copies the key material from the name-server service-metadata record into Route.echConfigList only for DIRECT (no proxy) routes; RouteSelector.nextRoutes then keeps only the routes that carry key material when any do, so there is no non-ECH fallback route.

ConnectPlan.connectTls passes route.echConfigList into Platform.configureTlsExtensions; only Android17SocketAdapter (Android SDK 37+) applies it with SSLSockets.setEchConfigList (an unparsable list is skipped), while the plain JVM platform ignores it.

CRITICAL: After an SSLException, ConnectPlan.nextConnectionSpec first asks Platform.echRetryPlan(exception); it gives up at once if this plan is already an ECH retry (only one ECH retry), and the production implementation Android10Platform.echRetryPlan returns a plan only on SDK 37+ for EchConfigMismatchException, built from the exception's public hostname and retry config list; the base Platform returns null.
EchRetryPlan.getOrNull returns null (no retry) when the public name cannot be canonicalised, is an IP address, or matches the invalid patterns (leading or trailing dot, numeric label).

CRITICAL: Before retrying, nextConnectionSpec verifies the retry plan's public name against the session certificate with route.address.hostnameVerifier and throws EchUntrustedException on failure; on success it returns a copy of the plan with a new Route carrying the retry config list (null means retry without ECH) and echRetryPlan set.

attemptAnotherConnection returns false only for EchUntrustedException, so FastFallbackExchangeFinder and SequentialExchangeFinder stop trying other plans and addresses; a successful retry plan is pushed with deferredPlans.addFirst and tried before other deferred plans.

probes.notes: VERIFICATION: RouteSelector.kt:184-193 (echRoutes filter, routesToTry), :253-258 (echConfigList only Proxy.Type.DIRECT); ConnectPlan.kt:354-361 (configureTlsExtensions with route.echConfigList), :214-217 (catch SSLException -> nextConnectionSpec), :501-541 (nextConnectionSpec: echRetryPlan!=null return null :507; Platform.get().echRetryPlan :509; hostnameVerifier.verify(publicName) :514-521 EchUntrustedException; copy(route=Route(...echConfigList=nextEchRetryPlan.configList)) :522-531); Android17SocketAdapter.kt:55-95 (setEchConfigList, InvalidEchDataException -> null); Android10Platform.kt:54-61 (adapter list), :93-102 (SDK_INT<37 / EchConfigMismatchException); Platform.kt:144 (default null); EchRetryPlan.kt:46-57 (getOrNull); RetryTlsHandshake.kt:31 (attemptAnotherConnection = e !is EchUntrustedException); FastFallbackExchangeFinder.kt:96,100-103; SequentialExchangeFinder.kt:46,57. DECOYS: EchRejectedException (ech/EchRejectedException.kt) is never thrown in production code: only the test platform okhttp-testing-support/.../FakeNetworkPlatform.kt:94-105 maps it; legacy AndroidPlatform.kt has no echRetryPlan override and no Android17 adapter; Jdk9Platform/ConscryptPlatform/BouncyCastle/OpenJSSE configureTlsExtensions take echConfigList but ignore it; Dns.Record.ServiceMetadata. probes.query: After a low-level network failure on an ordinary call, the client sometimes tries again (re-sends, uses another address, or uses a weaker TLS setup) and sometimes gives up. List every check that makes it give up, name where each lives, and say what exactly triggers it.
expectedFacts: RetryAndFollowUpInterceptor.recover gives up when the application disabled retries (chain.retryOnConnectionFailure is false, from the client setting or a per-call override).
recover gives up when the request send has started (the failure is not a ConnectionShutdownException) and the request body is one-shot or the failure is a FileNotFoundException.

RetryAndFollowUpInterceptor.isRecoverable returns false for ProtocolException, for InterruptedIOException unless it is a SocketTimeoutException before the request send started, for an SSLHandshakeException caused by a CertificateException, and for SSLPeerUnverifiedException; everything else is recoverable.

CRITICAL: RealCall.retryAfterFailure requires exchange.hasFailure and RealRoutePlanner.hasNext(failed connection) to be true; hasNext is true only with deferred plans, a pending next route, a retry route recovered from the failed connection (routeFailureCount == 0, noNewExchanges set, and same host reusable), or routes left in the current selection or selector; otherwise no retry.

ConnectPlan.nextConnectionSpec offers no further TLS configuration when this plan is already an ECH retry, when retryOnConnectionFailure is false, or when attemptAnotherConnectionSpec(e) is false (ProtocolException, any InterruptedIOException including connect timeouts, SSLHandshakeException caused by CertificateException, SSLPeerUnverifiedException, and any non-SSL exception); only other SSLExceptions move to the next compatible ConnectionSpec.
attemptAnotherConnection returns false only for EchUntrustedException, which makes both exchange finders abort instead of trying further plans or IP addresses.

probes.notes: VERIFICATION: RetryAndFollowUpInterceptor.kt:133-155 (recover: retryOnConnectionFailure :142; requestSendStarted :139, requestIsOneShot :145; isRecoverable :148; call.retryAfterFailure :151), :157-164 (requestIsOneShot: isOneShot || FileNotFoundException), :166-198 (isRecoverable); RealCall.kt:514-516 (retryAfterFailure: exchange?.hasFailure == true && routePlanner.hasNext(exchange?.connection)); RealRoutePlanner.kt:299-347 (hasNext, retryRoute: routeFailureCount != 0 -> null; !noNewExchanges -> null; canReuseConnectionFor); Exchange.kt:202-205 (trackFailure sets hasFailure); ConnectPlan.kt:501-541 (nextConnectionSpec), RetryTlsHandshake.kt:31-54; FastFallbackExchangeFinder.kt:96; SequentialExchangeFinder.kt:57. probes.query: A server-side JVM (not Android, not a native image) runs a Java 8 build from before the release that added built-in application-protocol negotiation. The first-registered security provider is an old Conscrypt release older than the minimum the code accepts, and the boot class path carries no add-on library for application-protocol negotiation. Which platform-adaptation class does the client end up using, what does it do when a connection configures TLS extensions, and which HTTP protocol do calls end up using? Several platform-selection routines exist; say which one applies.
expectedFacts: Selection happens in the jvmMain PlatformRegistry.findPlatform (not the androidMain registry and not the GraalSvm substitution): it checks whether the first security provider is named Conscrypt, then BC, then OpenJSSE, and each is used only if its buildIfSupported is non-null, otherwise it falls through.
ConscryptPlatform.isSupported requires the Conscrypt classes and atLeastVersion(2, 1, 0), so an older Conscrypt is not used.

Jdk9Platform.isAvailable is true only if java.specification.version parses as an int >= 9, or, when it does not parse (1.8), if SSLSocket has the getApplicationProtocol method (added in 8u251/252); here it is false.
Jdk8WithJettyBootPlatform.buildIfSupported returns null on Java 9+ or when the org.eclipse.jetty.alpn.ALPN classes are not on the boot class path.

CRITICAL: findPlatform returns the base Platform() (the open class) as the last fallback; its configureTlsExtensions is an empty no-op and getSelectedProtocol returns null, so ConnectPlan.connectTls sets protocol to HTTP_1_1 (no h2 negotiation).

probes.query: A developer configures a periodic liveness probe on the client to detect dead peers. Which kinds of connections actually send probes, how does the setting travel to the code that sends them, and what does the client do when an answer has not arrived by the time the next probe is due?
expectedFacts: The setting (OkHttpClient.pingIntervalMillis) reaches connections through RealCall.enterNetworkInterceptorExchange -> RealRoutePlanner -> ConnectPlan -> RealConnection, whose startHttp2 passes it to Http2Connection.Builder.pingIntervalMillis; it is used only for HTTP/2 (and h2 prior knowledge) connections, never for HTTP/1.1 connections.

CRITICAL: Http2Connection's init block schedules a periodic task on the writer queue; at each tick, if intervalPongsReceived < intervalPingsSent it calls failConnection(null), which closes the connection with PROTOCOL_ERROR (shutdown, cancels all open streams, cancels the socket); otherwise it increments the sent count and writes an INTERVAL_PING.
Web sockets use a separate mechanism: OkHttpClient.newWebSocket passes pingIntervalMillis to RealWebSocket, whose initReaderAndWriter schedules writePingFrame on its task queue.

CRITICAL: In RealWebSocket.writePingFrame, if the previous ping is still unanswered (awaitingPong) the web socket fails with SocketTimeoutException ('sent ping but didn't receive pong within ...ms'), delivering listener.onFailure and cancelling the socket; onReadPong resets awaitingPong.
Web socket handshakes force HTTP/1.1 (ONLY_HTTP1), so the HTTP/2 ping task never runs for web sockets.

probes.query: Compare two clients: a plain one, and one with the optional Brotli support added as an ordinary application-level interceptor. A caller asks for a byte range of a large file from a server that compresses whenever it is allowed to. For each client, say what compression the request advertises, who decompresses the answer, and what the caller receives if the server replies with a compression scheme the add-on does not know.
expectedFacts: BrotliInterceptor is CompressionInterceptor(Brotli, Gzip), registered as an application interceptor, so it runs before BridgeInterceptor in RealCall's chain.
CompressionInterceptor.intercept adds Accept-Encoding 'br, gzip' whenever its algorithm list is non-empty and the request has no Accept-Encoding of its own; it does not look at a Range header.

BridgeInterceptor advertises gzip (and later gunzips) only when the request has neither an Accept-Encoding nor a Range header; the plain client therefore advertises no compression for a range request and delivers the body untouched.
CRITICAL: With the add-on, the header is already present when the request reaches BridgeInterceptor, so Bridge does no gzip handling and the add-on's decompress step handles both br and gzip.

CRITICAL: CompressionInterceptor.decompress acts only if response.promisesBody() and Content-Encoding matches (case-insensitively) a configured algorithm; it then strips Content-Encoding and Content-Length and returns a streaming body of unknown length; an unrecognised encoding (for example deflate) is returned unmodified with Content-Encoding intact, so the caller gets compressed bytes.
If the caller sets its own Accept-Encoding, the add-on passes the request through and Bridge also leaves it alone, so the caller receives the raw compressed response.

probes.query: A caller fetches a list of parent records and asks that each parent's child records be loaded alongside them using one extra query for all parents (not a join). Starting from the moment the parent rows have been read, trace how this happens: which hook triggers it, when that hook does nothing, how the parent lookup keys are gathered, which callable fetches the children, and how each child ends up attached to its parent.
expectedFacts: Dataset#all builds the row array via _all, which calls post_load(rows) after loading and before any block; the generic Dataset#post_load does nothing.

CRITICAL: The model's association DatasetMethods#post_load calls eager_graph_build_associations when the dataset uses the join-based option, and calls eager_load only when the eager option is set AND (the dataset has a row_proc OR the join-based option is set); a naked dataset therefore skips separate-query loading.

eager_load returns for an empty row list, maps each requested name to its reflection (raising UndefinedAssociation for unknown names), calls prepare_eager_load then perform_eager_loads, and finally runs :after_load callbacks.

prepare_eager_load groups the parent rows by each reflection's eager_loader_key (primary key for one-to-many) into an id_map and builds a hash keyed by each reflection's :eager_loader callable; perform_eager_loads invokes every loader with its options hash.

CRITICAL: The one-to-many :eager_loader proc defined in def_one_to_many calls eager_load_results, which delegates to the reflection's eager_load_results; that initializes empty association caches on the parents and fetches all children in one query through the cached placeholder_eager_loader (WHERE key IN ids), unless a block or loader: false forces a freshly built eager_loading_dataset.

For each child the proc looks up the parents by the child's foreign key in id_map and pushes the child into each parent's association cache (or assigns it for one-to-one), also setting the reciprocal association.

probes.query: A model class is set up so that saving fails when another session changed the same row after it was loaded; the check relies on an integer revision column that the library raises on every update. Session A loads and saves. Session B, still holding the older copy, then saves. Trace how B's UPDATE gets restricted to the revision B holds, where the failure is detected, which exception class results, and what B's in-memory revision value and pending conditions look like afterwards.
expectedFacts: The optimistic locking plugin applies the optimistic_locking_base plugin, which applies the instance_filters plugin; the lock column defaults to lock_version.

CRITICAL: optimistic_locking_base's before_update (also before_destroy) calls lock_column_instance_filter, which registers an instance filter of lock_column => the revision value currently held in memory.
instance_filters overrides _update_dataset (and _delete_dataset) to apply the registered filters as extra WHERE conditions, so B's UPDATE matches only the row with the old revision.

CRITICAL: instance_filters.configure sets require_modification to true, so Model#_update raises NoExistingObject when the UPDATE did not modify exactly one row; the plugin's Error constant is that same Sequel::NoExistingObject.

optimistic_locking's _update_columns puts lock+1 into the column hash before calling super, and only after super succeeds does it write the new revision into the object; on failure B's in-memory revision stays at the old value.
The filters are cleared by after_update, after destroy and on refresh (_refresh); because after_update is not reached on failure, B's filter stays registered until it is refreshed.

probes.query: In which situations does the connection-pooling layer itself close a connection that it is tracking and then carry on, because that connection is broken, too old, idle for long and unresponsive, or because the thread that owned it is gone? Cover both the default behaviour and the optional add-ons; name each situation, its trigger, and what the pool does next. Do not count explicit user requests to disconnect.
expectedFacts: CRITICAL: In hold, an exception that is a DatabaseDisconnectError or a driver error classified by disconnect_error? makes the pool disconnect the connection, drop its allocation and call fill_queue(1) (timed queue), then re-raise the error; the failed operation is not retried.

When the pool is full and a new connection is needed, try_make_new (timed queue) and assign_connection (threaded) find connections allocated to threads that are no longer alive, remove them and disconnect them, then make room (the timed queue also calls fill_queue(count) so waiting threads get connections).

CRITICAL: The connection_validator extension's acquire checks a connection that has been idle longer than the validation timeout (default 3600 seconds), runs valid_connection?, and if the check is false removes the allocation, disconnects it via disconnect_acquired_connection and redoes acquisition to get another.

The connection_expiration extension's acquire disconnects any connection older than its expiration time (default 14400 seconds plus a random delay, set when the connection is made) regardless of health, then redoes acquisition.

The transaction_connection_validator extension turns a disconnect error raised while beginning a transaction into a DisconnectRetry (a DatabaseDisconnectError), so hold discards that connection; Database#transaction then retries with a new connection (at most 5 attempts in total) unless the retry would get the same connection, and otherwise raises the original database error.

probes.query: Which operations on a query object (not on the database object, and not on a single record) start a database transaction by themselves, without the caller wrapping them, and under what condition does each of them skip or avoid the transaction? Include operations that live in adapter-specific or optional-plugin code.
expectedFacts: CRITICAL: Dataset#paged_each runs its paging loop inside db.transaction(opts), which can be skipped with the :skip_transaction option; adapter overrides avoid it: the mysql2 adapter streams instead (no transaction) unless streaming is unsupported or stream: false, and the native PostgreSQL adapter pages through a cursor (see cursor_fetch_rows).

CRITICAL: Dataset#import (through _import_transaction) opens a transaction around multiple statements or per-row inserts, but sets skip_transaction when there is at most one value or statement; the PostgreSQL RETURNING branch of _import (and the MSSQL OUTPUT branch) uses no transaction at all.

The model dataset's destroy (model/base.rb) wraps all(&:destroy) in db.transaction, with skip_transaction when the model's use_transactions is false; the single_statement_dataset_destroy plugin's destroy opens its own transaction around the batch DELETE (unless around_destroy forces the default path).
PostgreSQL's Dataset#lock with a block starts a transaction, locks the tables and yields; without a block it only issues LOCK TABLE.

The native PostgreSQL adapter's cursor_fetch_rows (used when a cursor is requested) declares and fetches the cursor inside db.transaction, skipping it when the cursor is held (hold option / skip_transaction).

probes.query: Several model features can turn a duplicate-key problem on PostgreSQL into a validation-style error on the model. Which one only reacts after the database has already rejected the INSERT, uses the identity of the violated index reported by the driver to decide which model column to blame, and what does it do when it cannot map the violation? expectedFacts: CRITICAL: The pg_auto_constraint_validations plugin wraps _insert_raw, _insert_select_raw and _update_without_checking in check_pg_constraint_error, which rescues Sequel::ConstraintViolation raised by the database after the statement ran.
On rescue it calls the database's error_info (native postgres adapter, needs a 9.3+ server and client) to read schema, table, column, constraint name and primary message from the driver result.

For a UniqueConstraintViolation it looks the constraint name up in the unique-index metadata (gathered at set_dataset time with db.indexes, including partial indexes) and adds the configured message ('is already taken') to the mapped columns.

CRITICAL: If no column mapping is found, the metadata is missing, or the error's schema/table differs from the model's, errors are empty and the original database exception is re-raised; otherwise it raises ValidationFailed with the original exception as wrapped_exception.

The exception category UniqueConstraintViolation comes from the PostgreSQL error classification (database_error_regexps /duplicate key value violates unique constraint/ or SQLSTATE 23505), not from the plugin.

probes.query: On the embedded single-file SQL database adapter, when application code takes an exclusive row lock on a record it has already loaded, inside a transaction, so that other writers must wait, does the library send any row-locking clause to the database? If something close exists, say what it does instead.
expectedFacts: CRITICAL: SQLite's DatasetMethods#select_lock_sql is 'super unless @opts[:lock] == :update', so the FOR UPDATE lock style is silently omitted (the comment says this avoids raising errors for compatibility with other databases).
Model#lock! only calls _refresh on this.lock_style(style) (default :update), so on SQLite it reloads the row with a plain SELECT and takes no row lock.

The generic Dataset#select_lock_sql in dataset/sql.rb would append ' FOR UPDATE' for :update and appends a String lock style verbatim; the SQLite override suppresses only the :update symbol, so a raw string style would still be appended.

The nearest real concurrency control on SQLite is the transaction mode (begin_new_transaction uses opts[:mode] or the database's transaction mode: deferred, immediate or exclusive), which locks at database level, not per row.
